newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians welcome Socialist president with gunfire.
newsitem.headline: Albanians welcome Socialist president with gunfire.

text.p: Albanians fired deafening volleys into the air from looted weapons to celebrate the election of Socialist Rexhep Majdani as their president with the task of restoring order to the Balkan state.
State television broadcast an appeal from police for the shooting to stop, saying three policemen had been wounded already, as red tracer fire lit the Thursday night sky over Tirana.

Although a 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. curfew had been lifted, the city centre was virtually deserted as most people stayed in to watch the day's parliamentary proceedings on television. The celebratory gunfire erupted when the broadcast reached Majdani's swearing in.
Majdani's first act as president was to accept the resignation of interim prime minister Bashkim Fino and to ask Socialist Party chairman Fatos Nano to form a government.
Nano, who was expected to present his cabinet lineup on Friday, has said he will form a five-party coalition government following his party's decisive win in June 29 elections.

Apart from restoring security, its main task will be to sort out the economic chaos left by the collapse of high-interest pyramid schemes and put the Europe's poorest country on the road to reconstruction and modernisation.
His party campaigned in part on a promise to compensate pyramid investors who lost their life savings early this year -- a promise its opponents are unlikely to let the government escape.

Nano, 44, who had been jailed on corruption charges that his Socialists say were politically motivated, insists his reformed party has nothing to do with the Stalinist regime of Enver Hoxha who ruled for 40 years until his death in 1985.
Hoxha's successor, communist president Ramiz Alia, ruled out change but anti-government protests from July 1990 led to reforms culminating in multi-party elections in March 1991.
The Socialists and their coalition allies have 119 seats in the new 155-seat parliament, while the Democrats of outgoing president Sali Berisha have 27.
Parliament voted on Thursday to lift a state of emergency imposed on March 2 and then elected Mejdani, a former physics professor who joined the Socialist party only last year, as president.
"I call on all Albanians to help me realise my mission on the difficult road of normalising the life of the country and its institutions," Mejdani said in his acceptance speech.
"I call on all Albanian immigrants wherever they are to come back and contribute to the reconstruction of Albania."
Mejdani, 52, says proudly that unlike Nano and Berisha he was never a member of the once all-powerful communist party.

Berisha was initially welcomed for his pro-Western reform policies, but his increasingly authoritarian style lost him support and the collapse of the risky pyramid investment schemes early this year proved the final straw.
His government resigned in March at the height of civil disorder in which armouries were broken into and weapons and explosives stolen.
Large areas of the country, particularly in the south, are still at the mercy of armed gangs and even peaceable citizens keep a gun at home for self defence.
